results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 42 draft units match the controlling ideas of p01-p42 in spec order; the three callout entries match no spec paragraph (house callout). p37's summary carries an extra idea (see one_controlling_idea_per_paragraph) but its main idea matches.

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong ¶3
results.quote: One more gap belongs here: Adyen states that "Data changes to the legal entity of the account holder do not trigger webhooks", so the record is re-read after every change the platform submits
results.finding: The outliner needed two summaries for this unit: requirements the platform cannot satisfy, and Adyen's legal-entity changes emitting no webhooks (a stale-record problem). The second idea comes from the spec's own evidence list for p37, whose controlling idea does not cover it; the item belongs with the record and its re-read (p22) or nowhere.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: p01-p09 pose the problem (S1, S3), p10-p12 S1, p13-p19 S2, p20-p24 S3/S4, p25-p27 S5, p28-p29 S2/S3/S5, p30-p34 S1/S2/S4, p35-p37 S2/S4, conclusion synthesises S1-S5; p03 is the book's placing device and ties verification to the followed payment.

Figures 1-4 each carry a caption saying what they show and are introduced or followed by the point they make; the three-ways table is introduced (control vs upkeep, last column = judgement) and read in p19; the stages table is read in p26-p27; the comparison table is read in p29 (including the 'typically' Stripe periods: 'its typical periods are not fixed'). Quotations are followed by what they mean (e.g. p09 'The platform inherits the deadline', p16 'own forms also mean...', p25 'That is a vendor's claim about a redesign, not a completion rate').

results.draft_locus: Two Ways to Lose a Seller ¶1
results.quote: Two terms carry the rest of the chapter.
results.finding: Declared: elaboration of the review's two findings (form: paragraph) into the vocabulary and two ways to lose a seller. The section opens on the terms with no pickup of the review's findings, and the two halves just named (how data is collected / what happens after sign-up) are not related to the two losses that follow (drop-off at sign-up / restriction after it). Flow reader A (A2) re-read to separate the two pairs.

All other boundaries express the declared relationship and pick up the declared known information: p02 cause_effect ('Those nine days follow from the previous chapter's result'), p03 place, p04 sequence, scene example ('Start with what Ravi Shah could see'), p06 cause_effect, p08 cause_effect, p09 contrast, p10 problem_solution ('To reduce the loss at sign-up'), p11 cause_effect, p12 additional_support, p13 sequence, p14 example, p15 and p16 contrast, p17 elaboration, p18 conclusion_summary, p19 cause_effect, p20 time, p21 cause_effect, p22 problem_solution, p23 additional_support, p24 sequence, p25 contrast, p26 problem_solution, p27 elaboration, p28 conclusion_summary, p29 cause_effect, p30 example, p31 elaboration, p32 sequence, p33 time, p34 additional_support, p35 contrast, p36-p37 additional_support, p38-p40 label phrases, p41 under its house heading, p42 sequence.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶3
results.quote: This chapter comes before the first step of Mila Janssen's class pass. Studio Noord could take her €120.00 on Tuesday 9 March 2027
results.finding: Both readers stopped here: a second customer, studio, provider and a 2027 date arrive between the Ironworks thesis and the roadmap, are not tied to Ironworks and never return, so each had to work out whether Studio Noord was related. The spec places this unit here; a bridging clause tying the followed payment to the chapter's seller (or moving the note after the roadmap, a spec change) would fix it.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Collect the Data: Hosted, Embedded, API ¶5
results.quote: On Stripe there is a further rule about who may collect at all.
results.finding: Both readers read the API option as open to any Stripe platform and then had to re-read p16 when this rule (collect only if the platform bears losses and has dashboard none) arrived after it. The spec deliberately puts the rule after the design it restricts; a forward pointer in p16 might suffice, otherwise the order itself must change.

results.draft_locus: After Sign-Up: An Owner for Every Deadline, a Reason for Every Seller ¶5
results.quote: A periodic review arrives the same way, as error 3_10 with a deadline, and is closed by a call to `/legalEntities/{id}/confirmDataReview` once the seller has confirmed the data.
results.finding: The paragraph is about what the seller sees and does, and ends on an error code and an API endpoint; both readers lost the level. The spec's evidence allows the point, but the prose should give it from the seller's side (the review shows up as an open item with a date; the seller confirms the data) and keep the endpoint out of the closing sentence.

results.draft_locus: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
results.quote: Every Stripe and Adyen cell is a fact cited in this chapter, from documentation accessed in November 2026 unless a year is given, or says "Not public"; the last column is my reading, an inference.
results.finding: The promise is broken by the same paragraph and table: the pause rule and Adyen's `enabled` flag are new here, and Stripe's 'typically' 14/28-day periods for Custom accounts appear only in a table cell, never in the after-sign-up deadline discussion. Both readers went back looking for where these had been cited. Reword the promise to name the new cells, and state Stripe's typical periods in the prose with their source.

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: Onboarding Ironworks Climbing, and Keeping It Verified ¶2
results.quote: Payouts need no capability of their own on this account type; Stripe's Accounts v2 API requests them automatically for an account set up to take payments.
results.finding: Contradicts, on first reading, the definition example 'receiving payouts' (p07) and the hand-off's 'capabilities to receive payments and payouts are active' (p42); both readers re-read to reconcile. The account type is never named. Say which account type and API version this is and how payouts are enabled on it.

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: Onboarding Ironworks Climbing, and Keeping It Verified ¶4
results.quote: Replay May 2026 from Ravi's side. On the day Stripe announces the changed requirement, his back office shows a banner
results.finding: The counterfactual replay is in the present tense, mixed with present-tense facts that are true now (Jonas owns every deadline, the studio counts), so both readers could not tell at first whether this happened, happens now or would have happened. Mark the replay as hypothetical (would) and separate it from current facts.

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: Onboarding Ironworks Climbing, and Keeping It Verified ¶4

Both readers lost track of which studios are on which provider. State the split once (Dutch and German studios signed before 2024 on Stripe, later ones on Adyen) before the numbers.

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: Onboarding Ironworks Climbing, and Keeping It Verified ¶5

Every term on does_not_know is defined at first use in the body: capability and verification requirement (p07), beneficial owner (p10), up-front, incremental and staggered collection and payment facilitator (p12), hosted, embedded and API onboarding (p13), KYC and chargeback (p17). Keel, K6 and Larkfield's people are on already_knows. No flow reader reported a term as unexplained; the account-type confusion at p31 is recorded under flow_is_followable.
Opens on a vivid, dated anecdote (Ironworks' nine days), derives the thesis from the previous chapter's result, and gives a roadmap; none of the weak patterns.
The conclusion sorts what is established, what depends on context and the author's synthesis; it does not open with 'in conclusion', introduce a new subtopic or end on the thesis alone.

p40 states what no section states (collecting and keeping are one question: where the current requirement lives; the Frozen Studios failed on both) and why it matters: provider holds the form, platform holds the deadline with an owner and measures its own sign-up because no benchmark exists, turning nine days into a task of minutes.
p40: 'Ravi Shah's nine days become a banner with a date and a task of a few minutes' returns to the nine days without a reason.

The cold reader predicted all nine sections in order (guessing the two ways to lose a seller and the third collection method correctly), the evidence (dated provider documentation, the Larkfield case, explicit absence of completion figures, comparison tables) and the plain, sourced, prescriptive tone.

The reader explains the stop as a reopened requirement whose deadline passed, payouts stopping first (Stripe typically disables payouts; Adyen 30 vs 60 days), and names the record of open requirements, deadlines and capability status from account creation, a named owner, a watched channel to someone who can act, and a seller screen with reason, date and the provider's link or component. Matches expected.

The reader names keeping the forms current (Stripe: integration changes, review at least every six months, per country) and handling sellers' identity documents, plus the Stripe loss-bearing configuration. Matches expected.

p25 states that no completion rate or comparison is public for either provider (searched November 2026) and presents the 24 June 2019 Stripe figure with an evidence-age note as 'a vendor's claim about a redesign, not a completion rate'.
